job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Kira Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents and my little brother in a flat above my parents' pharmacy in Linden Road. Mornings I help with the stock count before opening, then I'm at my laptop by ten. I use AI all day, to tailor applications, to explain job descriptions I don't understand and to review my embedded-systems code. I finished a computer engineering degree seven months ago, top of the class, and my final project was a low-power sensor that tracks cold-chain temperatures for medicines. I interned at a medical-device firm and at a chip design start-up, and I still have no offer, which is baffling and humbling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit of a relief, and a bit of a letdown, since I've built my skills around these tools. I'd tell friends the tools are still useful even if the hype was silly. Online I'd post about practical ways I use them, not predictions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means a normal market, which is a slow one for graduates. I've applied to 100 jobs and had eight interviews. Two firms said I was a close second. I have about six weeks of savings and a loan of about nine thousand, and my parents would help in a pinch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on applications but start offering a free two-week pilot to small firms: I'd set up temperature monitoring for their stock. That gets me in the door and onto their payroll if they like it. I'd also keep refining my cold-chain sensor so I can sell it to pharmacies like my parents' one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless, but curious. I feel like I'm on a runway, just waiting for the plane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a free pilot. What's the idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Instead of asking them to trust a CV, I show them a working monitor in their own stock room. Pharmacies and small clinics lose stock to fridge failures all the time. My parents lost about 800 worth last winter, and nobody noticed until morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your parents react if you started a business instead of getting a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum would say get a salary first, and Dad would quietly want me to. But they also watched me build the sensor in the kitchen. I think they'd back me if I could show a few paying customers before I quit looking for jobs.

say: I'd say it's a **relief and a letdown**, since my skills are built around these tools.
I'd post **practical** ways I use the tools, not predictions.
think: A normal market is a **slow** one for graduates: 100 applications and two close seconds.
My cold-chain sensor solves a **real problem**, like my parents' 800 loss last winter.
do: Offer small firms a free two-week **monitoring pilot** with my sensor.
Keep refining the **cold-chain sensor** to sell to pharmacies.
Keep sending **applications** each week alongside it.
feel: Restless but **curious**, like waiting for a plane on a runway.
S0.quote: Instead of asking them to trust a CV, I show them a working monitor in their own stock room.
fieldNote: Kira treats the job hunt as a **product problem**: show, don't tell.
Her **parents' pharmacy** is her first test customer and her safety net.
Uses AI daily and sees no **conflict** with the hunt.

steps.text: Offer three local pharmacies a free two-week temperature monitoring pilot
Keep sending five applications a week to device and chip firms
Use AI to tune the sensor code and write the pilot reports

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a real shift, and I'd welcome it with caution. I'd tell friends to learn tools that let them do more with less, and not to compete on tasks a model can do cheaper. Online I'd say show your work and your judgement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For junior embedded and software jobs, a lot of what I do now is being done by tools. Entry roles will go to people who can design systems, test hardware and explain risk to a customer. That's a narrower door, but I think I'd fit through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd double down on the hardware side: boards, sensors, testing. I'd sell the sensor pilot as a small business on top of job hunting. I'd also take on small freelance firmware jobs through a platform, to build a record. And I'd write short posts about each build, so firms find me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly. I think I'm good at this kind of change, but I'd be lying if I said it didn't make my stomach flip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by narrower door?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer roles that say junior developer, more that say engineer with some hardware sense. Companies won't pay for ten juniors when one person with tools can ship the same code. I'd want to be that one person, or part of a team of three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Dan, who got a software degree and mostly does web pages. And my brother, who's fifteen and wants to code. I'd tell him to learn the hardware side and not just the app side.

I'd tell friends to show their **judgement** as well as their work.
think: The door for juniors gets **narrower**, but I'd fit through it with hardware skills.
Firms won't pay for ten juniors when **one person with tools** can ship the same.
do: Double down on **boards, sensors and testing**.
Take small **freelance firmware** jobs through a platform to build a record.
Write short **posts** about each build so firms find me.
feel: **Excited**, though my stomach flips a bit.
S1.quote: Companies won't pay for ten juniors when one person with tools can ship the same code.
fieldNote: Kira's adaptiveness shows: she moves toward **hardware** because it's harder to automate.
Worry for **Dan** and her brother shows she thinks beyond herself.
She wants to be the **one person with tools** inside a small team.

steps.text: Take small firmware freelance jobs through an online platform
Build two new board designs and test them with AI help
Take an online course in hardware safety and certification
Apply to medical-device and sensor firms as a hardware-minded engineer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is quick, but I'm oddly not panicked, and I'd say so. I'd tell friends to do two things: get any income now, and build something they own. Online I'd say we need retraining money and some clear rules on what firms can automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does mean my degree's thinking side is worth less every month. Robots for hands-on work come around 2031, so the physical side buys me maybe three years. A medical sensor I've designed myself is something to sell in that gap, because I own it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take whatever paid job comes first and put the sensor into production with a small manufacturing partner. I'd ask my parents to be my first customer and a reference. I'd also start a savings habit with half of every payment, because I'd expect a rough year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but sharp. I wouldn't sleep well, and I'd get a lot done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not panicked. What keeps you from it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Having a plan. I've seen people freeze, and it's worse than the thing itself. I'd rather move, even in the wrong direction at first, since you can correct a course but not a standstill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the plan look like in money terms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A first job pays about 30,000, and I'd put half of any sensor revenue into savings. If I sold fifty sensors at 120 each, that's 6,000. It's not wealth, but it covers my loan payments for a year.

say: I'd say get **any income** now and build something you own.
I'd back **retraining money** and clear rules on what firms can automate.
think: The thinking side of my degree is worth less **every month**, but the hardware side buys three years.
A sensor I **own** is something to sell in that gap.

Save **half** of every payment against a rough year.

fieldNote: Kira's coping tool is a **plan**; she says a standstill is worse than a wrong direction.

steps.text: Take the first paid job offered and keep the sensor project going
Put the sensor into production with a small manufacturing partner
Save half of every sensor payment
Ask my parents to be the first paying customer and reference

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a good amount of time, and I'd say people should use it. I'd tell friends to go on thinking about what they own, not only what they do. Online I'd say retraining credits should work like a bank account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is long enough to build a small company or a serious career. If the sensor gets traction, I'd have two years of revenue before AGI arrives and three more before robots. If it doesn't, I'd have a track record from the freelance work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a medical-device job for stable income, and run the sensor business on evenings and weekends. I'd hire a student part-time in year two. I'd use AI heavily to handle support, invoices and testing. By year three I'd decide whether to go full time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Optimistic, with a note of caution. It's a good kind of busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you go full time on your own business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Revenue that covers my own wages for six months, plus two customers who'd renew. Also my parents saying go. I'd ask them to tell me honestly, and they would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the part of that plan you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Support. A pharmacy needs the sensor to work at 3 a.m. If something breaks and I'm asleep, I lose their trust. I'd want a tiny rota of two or three people so I'm not the only phone number.

I'd say retraining credits should work like a **bank account**.
think: Five years is long enough to build a **small company** or a serious career.
If the sensor takes off I'd have **two years** of revenue before AGI arrives.

S3.quote: A pharmacy needs the sensor to work at 3 a.m. If something breaks and I'm asleep, I lose their trust.
fieldNote: Kira sets her own **decision rule** for going full time: six months of wages and two renewals.

steps.text: Take a medical-device engineering job for steady income
Run the sensor business evenings and weekends
Use AI to handle support tickets, invoices and testing
Put the first sensor revenue into stock and tooling

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fifth picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is generous, and I'd tell people to use it, not coast. I'd say governments should run pilots with retraining accounts and track what works. Online I'd write about building a business slowly and honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fine, probably, if I'm honest. Ten years lets me do a part-time master's, run the business and still have a life. The first year is the one to get through, since I'm not earning yet, but after that I'd have time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job by spring, then grow the sensor business, maybe hire two people by year five. I'd do a master's in embedded systems part-time and keep helping my parents' pharmacy. I'd also support my brother's coding, steering him toward hardware.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Hopeful. I'd actually enjoy that decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently from the people around you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd treat my skills as a portfolio, not a ticket. A degree is a ticket, and tickets expire. A portfolio of products, skills and customers is something I can keep rebuilding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the main thing that could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A repeat of this year: no job and a long wait. If that came in year one of the ten, I'd lean on the business and my parents. The long runway only helps if I make it through the first stretch.

I'd write online about building a business **slowly and honestly**.

Do a part-time master's in embedded systems

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, though less than most would. What I'd need is a way to keep earning while I build something of my own: retraining accounts, a small business grant and rules that keep firms hiring graduates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm more worried than I look. I use the tools every day and I feel good with them, but I also know it's easy to be the person who trains their own replacement. I'd like to be the one who owns the thing, not the one who runs it.

headlineQuote: I'd like to be the one who owns the thing, not the one who runs it.
portrait: Kira is a 23-year-old **computer engineering** graduate, top of her class, living above her parents' pharmacy.
She has made 100 applications and eight interviews, with six weeks of savings and a **nine thousand** loan.
She is a centrist and an early adopter, using AI daily and moving toward **hardware** and her own cold-chain sensor.
She would test the sensor with her parents' pharmacy and sell small pilots, backing it with a **salaried** job.
Her fear is training her own replacement; her answer is to **own** something.
biggestWorry: The two-year **AGI** picture worries her most, though a plan eases it more than for most.
whatWouldHelp: She wants retraining **accounts**, a small business grant and rules keeping firms hiring graduates.
